Alright, I've just finished a series of edits to `src/tui.tsx`. The most recent changes added a `streamBufRef` and a `queueRef` to buffer streaming deltas and queue user input while a turn is running, respectively. I also tweaked the `useEffect` that drives the spinner, elapsed time, TPS, and now also throttles the stream flush, and I added logic in the `submit` callback to push input onto the queue when `running` is true. The goal of all these modifications is to make the UI more stable: the input line should stay visible and not get overwritten by rapid token streaming, and any user input entered mid‑run should be queued and processed after the current turn finishes.

Now I need to verify that these changes actually work in practice. The best way is to compile the TypeScript code, build the binary, install it, and then run the TUI in an isolated environment where I can programmatically send input and capture the output. Since this is a CLI tool, using `tmux` to spawn a detached session is ideal: I can start `glint` with `--no-intro` (to avoid the banner clutter), send a prompt like “write a haiku about terminals”, and then capture the pane contents to see whether the input line remains visible while the model is streaming its response.

First, I should type‑check the project to catch any lingering type errors before I try to build. The repository uses `bun`, so `bunx tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit` will run the TypeScript compiler without emitting files. If that succeeds, I can proceed to the actual build step: `bun build src/index.tsx --compile --outfile dist/glint`. I don’t need the full build output, just the final line which will tell me whether the build succeeded or if there were any errors, so I’ll pipe the output through `tail -1`.

Assuming the build succeeds, the resulting binary will be placed in `dist/glint`. I want to make it globally accessible for the test, so I’ll copy it to `~/.local/bin/glint`. Before doing that, I should clean up any stray `tmux` session named `glint` that might be left over from a previous run; `tmux kill-session -t glint` will do that, and I’ll silence any errors with `2>/dev/null`. A short sleep (`0.8s`) gives the system a moment to settle after killing the session.

After copying the binary, I’ll echo `OK` so I have a clear marker in the tool output that the install step completed. Then I’ll start a fresh detached tmux session named `glint`, with a reasonable terminal size (`-x 110 -y 38`) and a working directory of `/tmp/glint-test`. Inside that session I’ll run `glint --no-intro`, redirecting any error output to `/tmp/glint-tui-err.log` so that I can inspect it later if needed.

Once the TUI is up, I need to give it a moment to initialize (`sleep 1.5`). Then I’ll send the test prompt: `write a haiku about terminals`. I’ll send the keys to the tmux session, followed by an `Enter`. A brief pause (`0.2s`) ensures the command is registered, then another short wait (`1.5s`) allows the model to generate a response. Finally, I’ll capture the pane contents with `tmux capture-pane -t glint -p`, filter out empty lines (`grep -v '^\s*$'`), and show the last 10 lines (`tail -10`) to see the generated haiku and verify that the input line remained visible throughout.

All of this can be expressed as a single Bash command, which the `bash` tool can execute. I’ll include a descriptive `description` field so it’s clear what this command is intended to do: “Build, install, verify input stays visible while running”.
